results.authors: Louis DN, Perry A, Wesseling P, et al.
results.key_finding: WHO 2021 integrates histology and molecular markers for CNS tumor classification. Astrocytoma, IDH-mutant, WHO grade 3 (anaplastic astrocytoma) is defined by IDH mutation and anaplastic histologic features (high mitotic index, nuclear atypia) without the microvascular proliferation or necrosis required for grade 4. IDH-wildtype diffuse astrocytic tumors are classified as glioblastoma regardless of histologic grade if TERT promoter mutation, EGFR amplification, or +7/-10 copy number change is present.

results.authors: Law M, Yang S, Wang H, et al.
results.key_finding: Relative cerebral blood volume (rCBV) on perfusion MRI correlates with glioma grade. An rCBV threshold of 1.75 demonstrated high sensitivity and specificity for distinguishing high-grade (grades 3-4) from low-grade (grade 2) gliomas. MR spectroscopy with elevated Cho/NAA ratio above 2.0 further supports high-grade neoplasm.
results.title: Glioma grading: sensitivity, specificity, and predictive values of perfusion MR imaging and proton MR spectroscopy

results.authors: Bulik M, Jancalek R, Vanicek J, et al.
results.key_finding: Elevated Cho/NAA ratio and presence of lipid-lactate peaks by 1H-MRS correlate with glioma grade. WHO grade 3 gliomas frequently show intermediate Cho/NAA ratios (2.0-4.0) and may lack the prominent lipid-lactate peaks characteristic of grade 4 glioblastoma, due to absence of established necrosis. MRS alone cannot reliably distinguish grade 3 from grade 4 without tissue confirmation.

patient.history_present_illness: Mr. Arjun Mehta is a 45-year-old right-handed software architect with a well-documented history of migraine without aura, in remission for the past three years on propranolol prophylaxis. He presents to the neurology inpatient service after an urgent outpatient MRI — ordered by his primary care physician — revealed a left frontoparietal mass. He first noticed a change in his headaches approximately six weeks ago: attacks became more frequent (daily to near-daily), the quality shifted from his typical unilateral throbbing migraines to a diffuse dull pressure that is worst upon awakening and persists through the morning, and his usual sumatriptan rescue provided only partial and transient relief. He initially dismissed the change as stress-related — he had recently taken on a demanding new project at work — and consulted his primary care physician, who increased the propranolol dose with no improvement. Three weeks ago, his wife noticed he was making uncharacteristic errors in everyday tasks: forgetting grocery items, losing his train of thought mid-sentence during dinner conversations, and failing to complete a weekly family financial review that he had managed without difficulty for years. On direct questioning, Mr. Mehta acknowledges mild word-finding pauses during high-pressure conversations but attributes them to fatigue. He denies any visual changes, limb weakness, or sensory symptoms. He has had no seizures and no episodes of loss of consciousness. He has lost approximately 3 kg over the past six weeks without intentional dietary change, which he attributes to reduced appetite. He denies nausea, vomiting, or fever. His propranolol and sumatriptan doses were adjusted twice over the past month without benefit. Given the refractory and qualitatively altered headache pattern plus the emerging cognitive changes, his primary care physician ordered an MRI brain with gadolinium, which demonstrated a left frontoparietal non-enhancing to patchily enhancing infiltrative mass without definite central necrosis. The radiologist raised concern for a glioma and recommended inpatient evaluation. He was admitted to the neurology service for urgent workup.
